text:
1. PRIMARY DIAGNOSIS
- Safety-critical warning: A generator that stalls under load during summer peak testing can drop critical facility power unexpectedly; do not rely on this unit for emergency service until a loaded heat-soak test with recorded fuel pressure and shutdown data is completed.
- Root cause with confidence percentage: Most likely heat-related fuel delivery loss, usually a weak electric fuel lift pump or fuel supply restriction that worsens as fuel temperature rises, 72% confidence.
- The only code provided is ECU-1425. No auto-detected standardized DTCs were supplied, so this report treats ECU-1425 as the sole fault indicator from the customer data and does not invent any others.
- For ECU-1425: the monitor is typically tied to the engine/genset controller detecting an abnormal engine operating condition severe enough to command shutdown, commonly by comparing commanded fueling/governed speed against actual engine speed and protective inputs during loaded operation; it sets when the controller sees the engine can no longer maintain stable combustion or governed RPM under load and a shutdown threshold is crossed.
- For ECU-1425 failure physics: a healthy fuel system maintains positive supply pressure and adequate flow to the high-pressure side/injectors as fuel warms; when a lift pump weakens electrically or mechanically, or a suction-side restriction increases vacuum, hot low-viscosity fuel and underhood heat reduce net pump margin, rail/supply pressure falls, combustion energy drops, engine speed sags under load, controller interprets the event as an engine fault/shutdown condition, and the unit stalls; after 30 minutes cooling, pump winding resistance drops and vapor tendency decreases, allowing restart.
- ECU-1425 tied to this case data: the generator runs about 15 minutes, then stalls only under load, and restarts after cooling. That time-to-failure pattern is classic for thermal degradation rather than a static issue like low oil level or blocked vents, both of which the customer already checked.
- Two common misdiagnoses for ECU-1425 on this symptom pattern: replacing the coolant temperature sender because the event happens in summer, which is wrong unless recorded coolant temperature actually exceeds shutdown threshold in degrees and the controller log shows overtemp; replacing injectors because the engine dies under load, which is wrong unless supply pressure and return-flow tests prove the low-pressure side is healthy first.
- Single decisive verification test for ECU-1425: loaded hot fuel-supply pressure/flow test with a calibrated 0-15 psi fuel pressure gauge or electronic transducer and a data logger; expected reading is stable supply pressure within the engine’s published low-pressure spec during the full 15-20 minute load run, with no collapse below the minimum threshold specified by Cummins/engine documentation; fail is pressure dropping below spec as stall approaches or flow volume below spec during a timed container test.
- Component failure analysis: likely electrical degradation of the lift pump windings or commutator from age/heat, or contamination/restriction in the pickup, hose liner, tank vent, or filter head causing excessive suction vacuum when fuel demand rises under load.
- Age/hours considerations: this is a 2016 unit, so even without hours data, rubber hoses, pump brushes, relay contacts, and fuel shutoff solenoid coils are now old enough for heat-related intermittent failure. Lack of hours is a major missing variable because standby generators can age out components even with low runtime.

2. DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS
- 1) Heat-weakened fuel lift pump or suction restriction: most likely because the engine runs normally cold, fails after about 15 minutes under load, and restarts after a 30-minute cool-down. This alternative can produce the same ECU-1425 shutdown behavior and is where shops often misdiagnose by skipping pressure testing.
- 2) Fuel tank vent restriction or collapsing suction hose: highly plausible because summer heat and sustained load increase fuel draw; the ruling observation would be excessive inlet vacuum or immediate improvement when running with a known-good temporary fuel supply and vented cap arrangement.
- 3) Fuel shutoff solenoid or run relay coil opening when hot: plausible because coils can fail only at temperature; the ruling observation is loss of hold voltage or coil continuity exactly at stall, while fuel pressure may remain normal until the instant of shutdown.
- 4) Engine coolant overtemperature shutdown: possible but less likely because the customer reports cooling vents are clear, and the symptom is specifically under load in summer. It is ruled in only if logged coolant temperature reaches the controller’s shutdown threshold in degrees Fahrenheit/Celsius before stall. This can also present as ECU-1425-type shutdown behavior and is another common misdiagnosis.
- 5) Oil pressure switch/sender drifting hot: less likely because oil level is correct and the engine restarts after cooling, but a failing sender can falsely trigger shutdown. It is ruled in only if measured mechanical oil pressure remains normal while the controller input falsely drops out hot.
- 6) Ignition/ECM power supply dropout from heat-soaked relay or poor ground: possible on older standby equipment. The ruling observation is voltage at ECM B+ or ground drop changing beyond acceptable limits at stall.
- 7) Air intake restriction or exhaust restriction: less likely because the unit runs 15 minutes before failing and vents are clear, but a nesting issue or muffler collapse can show under load. It is ruled in by excessive intake restriction or exhaust backpressure readings.
- Equipment-specific pattern: standby generators often fail during summer peak tests because that is when enclosure temperature, fuel temperature, and electrical load are all highest; intermittent low-pressure fuel faults and hot relays are more common than catastrophic internal engine faults on units that restart cleanly after cooling.

3. DIAGNOSTIC VERIFICATION
- 1) Controller event log and shutdown parameter capture; tool required: Cummins PowerCommand/InPower-compatible service tool or OEM panel diagnostics; procedure: retrieve active/inactive events and record coolant temp, oil pressure, engine speed, battery voltage, and shutdown reason before and after a loaded run; expected reading is a specific shutdown reason with stable values until failure; fail is missing data or a parameter crossing shutdown threshold at stall; fair shop cost: 0.5-1.0 hr diagnostic time × prevailing heavy-equipment labor rate $140-$190/hr = $70-$190.
- 2) Loaded fuel supply pressure test; tool required: 0-15 psi liquid-filled gauge or electronic transducer with hose tee; procedure: tee into low-pressure supply at the engine/filter outlet and run the generator at the same summer peak test load until failure; expected reading is pressure staying within engine published low-pressure spec throughout the run, measured in psi; fail is pressure sagging below minimum spec or oscillating sharply just before stall; fair shop cost: 0.8-1.2 hr × $140-$190/hr = $112-$228.
- 3) Fuel supply vacuum restriction test; tool required: vacuum gauge/manometer on suction side; procedure: measure inlet restriction from tank to pump/filter during loaded operation; expected reading is suction vacuum below the engine/fuel-system maximum allowable restriction in inches Hg; fail is vacuum above spec, indicating blocked pickup, vent, hose, or filter head; fair shop cost: 0.5-0.8 hr × $140-$190/hr = $70-$152.
- 4) Temporary remote fuel source test; tool required: clean auxiliary diesel can, known-good hose, and safe temporary feed setup; procedure: run from a vented external fuel source to bypass tank pickup/vent/suction plumbing; expected reading is normal operation beyond the usual 15-minute failure point; fail is stall still occurs, ruling out tank-side restriction; fair shop cost: 0.5-0.8 hr × $140-$190/hr = $70-$152.
- 5) Hot fuel shutoff solenoid voltage and coil resistance test; tool required: DVOM and amp clamp; procedure: monitor hold voltage during loaded run and measure coil resistance cold versus hot immediately after stall; expected reading is steady battery voltage within about 0.5 V of charging voltage at the solenoid and coil continuity remaining intact; fail is voltage loss or open/high-resistance coil when hot; fair shop cost: 0.5-0.8 hr × $140-$190/hr = $70-$152.
- 6) Coolant temperature verification; tool required: scan data plus infrared thermometer/contact thermocouple; procedure: compare controller-reported coolant temperature to actual thermostat housing temperature during loaded run; expected reading is close agreement, typically within about 5-10°F; fail is false high reading or actual overtemp approaching shutdown threshold; fair shop cost: 0.5-0.8 hr × $140-$190/hr = $70-$152.
- 7) Mechanical oil pressure verification hot; tool required: mechanical oil pressure gauge; procedure: verify actual oil pressure at operating temperature and load; expected reading is above the engine’s minimum hot oil pressure spec in psi; fail is actual pressure dropping below spec or sender disagreement; fair shop cost: 0.5-0.8 hr × $140-$190/hr = $70-$152.
- Total diagnostic budget line: fair total for a disciplined diagnosis is $392-$1,178 based on 2.8-6.2 hr total diagnostic time × prevailing heavy-equipment labor rate $140-$190/hr, depending on how quickly the fault reproduces under load.
- The ONE test that must be completed and shown to the customer BEFORE any part is purchased: the loaded hot fuel-supply pressure test with recorded psi versus time through the stall event.

4. SHOP INTERROGATION
- Question 1: “Please show me the controller event log and the exact shutdown reason recorded when ECU-1425 occurred.” Competent answer: they provide a printout or screen capture with timestamp, shutdown category, coolant temp, oil pressure, RPM, and battery voltage. Red-flag answer: “These generators don’t store anything useful” or “we cleared it already.”
- Question 2: “What was low-pressure fuel supply in psi at cold start, at 10 minutes under load, and at the moment before stall?” Competent answer: three recorded readings with the gauge/transducer location identified and the engine spec referenced. Red-flag answer: “Fuel pressure seemed okay” with no numbers.
- Question 3: “What was suction restriction in inches of mercury from tank to pump under load?” Competent answer: a measured inHg value compared to allowable restriction from service information. Red-flag answer: “The filter was changed last season so restriction can’t be it.”
- Question 4: “Did you verify actual coolant temperature against the sensor reading, and what was the temperature difference in degrees?” Competent answer: they show scan data and IR/thermocouple readings within a stated tolerance. Red-flag answer: “It’s summer, so it’s probably overheating.”
- Question 5: “What voltage did the fuel shutoff solenoid or ECM power feed have at stall, and do you have a meter capture?” Competent answer: recorded voltage stayed within a stated range or dropped out at failure, with the test point identified. Red-flag answer: “We usually replace the relay and solenoid together.”
- Specific artifacts they must physically show you: scan/service-tool report printout, recorded fuel pressure/vacuum values, temperature comparison notes or photos, and any removed parts retained for inspection.

5. CONVERSATION SCRIPTING
- Opening: “I’ve done some research and want to understand how you verified the shutdown cause before any parts are ordered.”
- Phrasing: “Out of curiosity, what did fuel pressure do as it approached the 15-minute stall point?”
- Example dialogue: “I’ve done some research and want to understand: can you show me the event log and the fuel-pressure readings in psi during the loaded run?”
- Example dialogue: “Out of curiosity, did you compare actual coolant temperature to the sensor reading, and what was the difference in degrees?”
- Response handling: “I’m not questioning your experience; I just want the measured values so I can approve the repair with confidence.”
- Exit strategy: “Thank you for your time. I’m going to hold off until I have the recorded readings and then I’ll decide how to proceed.”
- NEVER say: “My AI report says...” or “I got a second opinion online.”
- ALWAYS say: “I’ve done some research and want to understand...”

6. COST BREAKDOWN
- Because no shop quote was provided and the exact engine submodel/part numbers were not supplied, pricing is given as realistic market ranges for a 2016 Cummins standby-generator fuel-delivery diagnosis and repair.
- Itemized parts pricing, likely primary repair: electric fuel lift pump, OEM Cummins/Onan pricing typically $180-$420 published dealer/online OEM parts range; quality aftermarket equivalent where available typically $90-$220 published aftermarket supplier range.
- Itemized parts pricing, possible related items: fuel shutoff solenoid, OEM typically $120-$280 published dealer/industrial supplier range; quality aftermarket typically $60-$160 published aftermarket range.
- Itemized parts pricing, possible restriction repair items: fuel hose, clamps, pickup/strainer, and tank vent components typically $20-$180 total published parts range depending on what is actually failed.
- Labor for lift pump replacement: fair labor is 1.0-2.0 hr book/typical field time × prevailing heavy-equipment labor rate $140-$190/hr = $140-$380.
- Labor for fuel shutoff solenoid replacement: fair labor is 0.8-1.5 hr book/typical field time × $140-$190/hr = $112-$285.
- Labor for hose/pickup/vent correction: fair labor is 1.0-2.5 hr typical field time × $140-$190/hr = $140-$475, depending on access.
- Diagnostic fee norms: fair diagnosis is $392-$1,178 based on 2.8-6.2 hr × $140-$190/hr; on a repair of this type, at least part of the diagnostic fee should be credited toward the final repair if the same shop performs the work.
- Fair total price range for the most likely repair path: diagnosis plus lift pump replacement totals $712-$1,978 based on $392-$1,178 diagnostics + $180-$420 OEM pump or $90-$220 aftermarket pump + $140-$380 labor.
- OVERCHARGE LINE: above $2,571 for diagnosis plus lift-pump repair is excessive, calculated as 30% above the top fair total of $1,978.
- If the repair instead proves to be only a vent/hose restriction, fair total is $552-$1,833 based on $392-$1,178 diagnostics + $20-$180 parts + $140-$475 labor.
- If the repair proves to be a fuel shutoff solenoid, fair total is $624-$1,743 based on $392-$1,178 diagnostics + $120-$280 OEM or $60-$160 aftermarket + $112-$285 labor.

7. RIPOFF DETECTION
- Exact parts-cannon sequence shops run on this failure: first the fuel filter, then the temperature sender, then the shutdown relay, then the fuel shutoff solenoid, then injectors; each is a guess unless they can show the measured parameter that failed at the moment of stall.
- Why the filter is a guess: the customer already changed it last season, and a filter can still be bad, but only a pressure drop or restriction reading proves it.
- Why the temperature sender is a guess: summer operation suggests heat, but only actual coolant temperature versus sensor data proves overtemp or false reporting.
- Why the relay/solenoid is a guess: hot electrical failures happen, but they require captured voltage/resistance loss at stall.
- Why injectors are a guess: injector replacement without proving healthy low-pressure supply is classic overspend.
- Dollar thresholds specific to this repair: fair total for the likely lift-pump path is $712-$1,978 based on section 6; padding starts above $1,978 and outright gouging starts above the overcharge line of $2,571.
- Walk away NOW triggers: refusal to perform or show a loaded fuel-pressure test; “we replace the pump and solenoid as a set”; charging a diagnostic fee with no recorded readings; claiming ECU-1425 automatically means a specific part without test data.
- Line items to refuse outright for this job: “injector replacement due to stalling” unless supply pressure and return tests are documented; refusal line: “I’m not authorizing injectors until the low-pressure fuel system is proven within spec under load.”
- Line items to refuse outright for this job: “cooling system overhaul due to summer shutdown” unless actual overtemp is documented; refusal line: “Please show me the recorded coolant temperature crossing the shutdown threshold first.”
- Line items to refuse outright for this job: “relay/solenoid package replacement” without hot voltage-drop evidence; refusal line: “I’ll approve the failed component once you show the voltage or resistance loss at stall.”

8. AUTHORIZATION GUIDE
- Approve immediately: up to $392-$1,178 for a full recorded diagnosis based on 2.8-6.2 hr × $140-$190/hr, but only if it includes the loaded hot fuel-pressure test and event-log capture.
- Reject outright: any parts replacement before the shop shows recorded psi, temperature, voltage, or pressure data tied to the stall.
- Get a second opinion when: the first shop cannot reproduce the fault under load, cannot provide recorded values, or quotes above the $2,571 overcharge line for the likely lift-pump repair path.
- What the second shop must be told: “The unit stalls after about 15 minutes under load in summer and restarts after 30 minutes cooling; please perform a loaded fuel-pressure/vacuum test and capture shutdown data.”
- What NOT to tell the second shop: do not suggest the part you suspect, because that biases them toward parts-cannon behavior.

9. TECHNICAL EDUCATION
- System operation explanation: on a diesel generator, the governor/controller holds engine speed constant under changing electrical load by increasing fuel delivery. The low-pressure fuel system must continuously feed the injection system with adequate pressure and flow. If supply pressure falls, the engine cannot make enough torque to hold RPM, combustion weakens, speed droops, and the controller may command shutdown to protect the set or because speed/frequency falls out of range.
- ECU-1425 physics in plain language: the controller is not “seeing a bad part” directly; it is seeing an operating condition that no longer matches what a healthy engine should do. Under load, fuel demand rises. In summer, fuel and enclosure temperatures rise. Heat increases electrical resistance in pump windings and relay contacts, reduces magnetic force in weak solenoids, and can increase vapor tendency on the suction side. Any of those can reduce delivered fuel enough that the engine runs out of torque and dies.
- Why cooling restores operation: after 30 minutes, pump windings, relay coils, and sensors cool down, resistance drops, and marginal components work again temporarily. That thermal reset behavior is one of the strongest clues in your symptom set.
- Two common ECU-1425 misdiagnoses explained: shops often blame “overheating” because the event happens in summer, but true overtemperature must be proven with actual temperature data; they also blame “bad injectors” because the engine stalls under load, but injectors do not usually heal after a 30-minute cool-down in such a repeatable way unless the supply side is failing first.
- Decisive verification test explained: a pressure gauge on the low-pressure fuel line converts guessing into physics. If pressure starts normal and then falls below spec as the stall approaches, the fault is in supply delivery. If pressure stays in spec, attention shifts to shutdown controls, temperature, oil pressure, or electrical power to the run circuit.
- Prevention tips specific to this equipment and usage pattern: exercise the generator under meaningful load, not just idle/no-load, because heat-related faults only appear when fuel demand and enclosure temperature rise; replace aging fuel hoses and inspect tank venting on time-based intervals, not just hours; record baseline fuel pressure, coolant temperature, and oil pressure during a healthy summer load test so future drift is obvious.

10. OEM PARTS STRATEGY
- Specific part numbers when possible: exact part numbers cannot be stated honestly from the data provided because the RS20A generator package can be built with different engine/fuel-system components by spec and serial number; the shop should identify the pump/solenoid by model-spec and serial tag before ordering.
- Why OEM may be critical: for the lift pump and shutdown solenoid, OEM is preferred if the generator is mission-critical because pressure output, connector fit, and coil durability matter in hot enclosed operation.
- When aftermarket is acceptable: quality aftermarket hoses, clamps, and some generic relays can be acceptable if temperature rating, fuel compatibility, and terminal quality match OEM.
- Pricing sources and deltas: OEM pump typically runs $180-$420 published dealer/online OEM parts range versus $90-$220 aftermarket supplier range; OEM solenoid typically $120-$280 versus $60-$160 aftermarket supplier range.
- Best practice: if the diagnosis proves a pump failure, ask for the exact OEM part number from the Cummins/Onan parts catalog tied to your model-spec and compare that published price to the shop’s markup.

11. NEGOTIATION TACTICS
- Anchor on the numbers: “For this repair path, I understand the fair total is $712-$1,978 based on $392-$1,178 diagnosis, $180-$420 OEM pump pricing, and 1.0-2.0 hours at $140-$190 per hour. Please show me where your quote fits.”
- Labor justification question: “What book-time or standard are you using for this job, and what is your posted labor rate?”
- If they quote high labor: “Anything materially above 2.0 hours for a straightforward lift-pump replacement looks padded unless access is unusually difficult; please document the access issue.”
- Walk-away point in dollars: “If the quote for the likely lift-pump repair path is above $2,571 without extraordinary documented access or additional proven faults, I’m going to decline and get another shop.”
- Leverage play: authorize diagnosis only first, then approve parts only after the loaded pressure test is shown; this prevents the shop from burying guesses inside a bundled estimate.
- Leverage play: if the unit is not emergency-live right now, use timing flexibility to avoid rush charges and ask whether the diagnostic fee is credited to repair.
- Leverage play: decline bundled add-ons unrelated to the stall complaint unless they are supported by measured data from the same visit.

12. LIKELY CAUSES (RANKED)
- Primary cause: heat-related low-pressure fuel delivery failure, 72% confidence, because the unit stalls only after about 15 minutes under load during summer peak tests and restarts after cooling, which strongly matches a weak lift pump or suction restriction.
- Secondary cause: hot fuel shutoff solenoid/run-relay or ECM power-feed dropout, 18% confidence, because thermal electrical failures can mimic fuel starvation and also reset after cooling.
- Tertiary cause: actual or falsely reported overtemperature/oil-pressure shutdown, 10% confidence, because protective shutdowns can occur under summer load, but the customer’s note that vents are clear and the repeatable cool-down restart pattern fit fuel/electrical thermal faults better.

13. RECOMMENDATIONS
- Immediate actions required: do not rely on this generator for critical backup duty until a loaded hot-run diagnostic captures fuel pressure and shutdown data through the failure event.
- Future maintenance schedule: add an annual summer load-bank or real-load test with recorded fuel pressure, coolant temperature, oil pressure, and battery voltage; replace time-aged fuel hoses and inspect tank venting on a calendar basis given the 2016 age.
- Warning signs to monitor: longer crank time when hot, slight RPM hunting before stall, audible change in lift-pump sound, enclosure heat buildup, or immediate restart only after opening the enclosure and cooling.

14. SOURCE VERIFICATION
- Cummins Power Generation service literature portal for model/spec manuals, controller diagnostics, and parts identification by serial/model-spec: https://quickserve.cummins.com
- Cummins Onan generator manuals and service publications repository, useful for PowerCommand/Onan controller event interpretation and fuel-system test procedures by model/spec: https://www.cummins.com/generators/manuals
- SmokStak Onan/Cummins generator technical forum, an independent field-experience source with repeated hot-stall, fuel-pump, and shutdown-solenoid case studies on standby sets: https://www.smokstak.com/forum/forums/onan-generators.1/
- Specific bulletin note: exact TSB/service bulletin numbers cannot be cited responsibly without the generator’s full model-spec and serial number; those identifiers are required to pull the correct Cummins/Onan service bulletin set from QuickServe and avoid mismatching procedures.

15. NEXT STEPS SUMMARY
- Authorize diagnosis only, capped at the fair diagnostic range of $392-$1,178 based on 2.8-6.2 hr × $140-$190/hr, and require a recorded loaded fuel-pressure test plus controller event log before any parts are ordered.
- If fuel pressure drops below spec as the stall approaches, approve only the proven failed fuel-supply component and keep the total likely repair path within the fair range of $712-$1,978; walk away above $2,571 unless they document an additional proven fault.
- Gather the generator model-spec tag and serial number before parts ordering so the shop can identify the exact OEM pump/solenoid part number and pull the correct Cummins service procedure.
